Outreach · Senior Product Designer

From Passive Database to Active System

From passive database to active system — an AI sales command center that tells reps what to do next, and shows its reasoning.

Role
Principal Product Designer
Scope
Product strategy, UX architecture, AI system design
Surfaces
Queue, pre-call briefs, post-call review
Focus
Trust, automation boundaries, adoption
~6 hrs
Admin time reclaimed per rep, per week
$13K–22.5K
Recovered productivity per rep, annually
20–40x
ROI at a $49–59/user/month price point
99%
CRM sync accuracy, human-reviewed

The problem I kept hearing

Talk to enough sellers and you hear the same complaint in different words: "The CRM only tells me what I already know." It's a system of record — it remembers what happened, but it never tells you what to do next. Reps carrying 15–25 active deals were spending hours every week feeding it data it should have been able to infer on its own.

Prioritization

Paralysis by wall of notifications

Reps opened their day to unread threads and open deals with no signal about what actually mattered right now.

Pre-call

The same sleuthing, every single time

1–2 hours before every kickoff call, piecing together history from email, old transcripts, and CRM notes.

Post-call

6–8 hours a week of fragmentation

Writing summaries, logging tasks, drafting follow-ups, and updating fields by hand, after every call.

None of this was a data problem. The CRM already had everything — email threads, calendar, call transcripts, pipeline history. It just never did anything with it. That was the reframe I wanted the team to work from: stop treating the CRM as a place sellers report into, and start treating it as a system that works for them.

The bet I made on architecture

I made an early, deliberate call: this couldn't be a bolted-on assistant living in its own tab. Every meeting-notetaker on the market already does summaries — that's table stakes, not a differentiator. The thing nobody was doing well was using native CRM context to act before and during the deal, not just after the call ended. So I architected the workspace around a single AI synthesis layer sitting underneath three surfaces sellers would actually live in.

CRM Data + Email + Calendar + Meeting Transcripts
AI Synthesis & Decision Engine
Prioritized Queue
30-Sec Pre-Call Briefs
Human-in-the-Loop Post-Call Workflows

1. A queue that shows its reasoning

Instead of another sortable task list, I designed a single prioritized queue that continuously re-ranks itself against signals from meetings, email, and pipeline movement. The part I fought hardest for was what I ended up calling the "Why" engine — every surfaced action carries a visible, specific explanation for why it's there.

It was tempting to ship the ranking without the reasoning — it's simpler, and the model's confident either way. But a queue that just tells you what to do without showing its logic trains people to either blindly comply or ignore it entirely, and neither builds the trust this product needed to survive daily use. Showing the "why" turns the queue into something a rep can argue with — which is exactly what makes it trustworthy.

2. Killing the pre-call scramble

The pre-call brief pulls deal history, recent threads, past call notes, and flagged risks into one view a rep can absorb in under 30 seconds instead of the 1–2 hours it used to take. Competitively, this was the differentiator I was most confident in — most tools in this category are built for after the call. Only about a third of direct competitors offer anything comparable before one.

3. Automating the admin, not the judgment

Post-call, the system drafts four things automatically: a summary, extracted follow-up tasks, draft follow-up emails, and recommended CRM field updates. This is the highest-leverage part of the product financially — and also the riskiest. It's the part most likely to quietly corrupt someone's pipeline data if I got it wrong.

The trust problem I designed around

The failure mode I was most worried about wasn't the AI being wrong — it was the AI being wrong silently. Misfiled records, inaccurate field updates pushed straight into the CRM, automations running with no visible seam for a human to catch a mistake. That's the pattern that kills adoption of AI tools in CRMs specifically, because the CRM is the system of truth for the entire revenue org.

Drafts

Automation drafts, humans approve

Nothing writes to the CRM without a person confirming it first.

Traceability

Every AI claim is clickable

Summaries and suggested field updates link straight to the exact timestamp in the transcript or email they came from — no black-box trust required.

One surface

One review drawer, not five

Reps approve, edit, or reject everything in a single place before anything syncs, instead of chasing confirmations across separate flows.

It would have been faster to ship with more automation and less friction up front. I chose the friction deliberately — the cost of one badly polluted deal record is much higher than the cost of one extra click.

Positioning it against what already existed

I also had to design this to sit clearly between two existing categories, not compete head-on with either.

Standalone notetakersFathom, Fireflies CI dashboardsGong, Chorus Nova
FocusPost-call summariesManager-level analyticsDaily execution
CRM integrationBolted-on, easy to misfileRead-heavy, complexNative, zero placement errors
Pre-call intelligenceMinimalInsight-onlyAutomated briefs
Interaction modelManual copy-pasteSeparate tabOne workspace, human-in-the-loop
Notetakers own the summary. CI tools own the analytics. Neither owns the moment where a rep actually decides what to do next — that gap is where I designed this to live.

What I'd change next time

  • Acceptance rate alone isn't the signal that matters — every edit or rejection is worth more.
  • Instrumenting disagreement early is the fastest way to catch model drift before it costs trust.
  • The review drawer should make the system smarter over time, not just safer on day one.
  • Friction you chose deliberately is still worth re-measuring as adoption and trust grow.
Outreach · Senior Product Designer

Research Agent

Fusing first-party conversation data with live web research into one agent that plans accounts, personalizes outreach, and catches risk before it becomes churn.

Role
Design lead, end-to-end
Team
Product, Design, Data Science, Applied AI
Surfaces
Accounts, Account Plan, Sequences
Focus
Targeting, personalization, risk

Reps and account teams already sit on a goldmine of first-party signal — calls, emails, meetings — but most of it evaporates the moment a call ends. Account plans go stale, territory research happens in a dozen browser tabs, and personalization gets skipped because there simply isn't time. I proposed a Research Agent that combines that first-party conversational intelligence with live external web research, so a team gets one auto-populated account plan instead of ten open tabs.

The agent works across three jobs at once: it segments and targets accounts, personalizes outreach around each account's actual pain points, and auto-populates the account plan — engagement strategy, key personas, barriers, mitigation — while surfacing risk signals a rep might otherwise miss until it's too late to act on them.

I proposed this now because the competitive ground was shifting fast. Without an AI capability at this depth, Outreach risked being seen as a capable but basic back-office tool next to a new wave of AI-native sales platforms. This wasn't just a feature — it was a hedge against commoditization, a lever toward consumption-based billing, and the start of a data flywheel: the more a team uses it, the sharper its insights get, and the more of the platform they end up adopting.

Project highlights
Challenge

Insight, scattered everywhere

Account context lived in calls, emails, meetings, and the open web — never in one place, and never current.

Approach

One agent, two data worlds

Paired Outreach's first-party conversational intelligence with external web research into a single generated account plan.

Outcome

A moat competitors can't buy

A research capability for full-cycle sellers not yet offered by Gong, Salesloft, Clari, or Groove.

What sets it apart

Heavyweight competitors like Gong, Salesloft, Clari, and Groove have conversational intelligence. Smaller, newer players offer web-research features. Almost none of them have both — and the ones that come close don't have years of first-party call and email data to ground their research in. That combination is what makes the output feel relevant to a specific deal, not just generically well-researched.

That gave us a genuine first-mover position: the first comprehensive research capability built for full-cycle sellers, aimed squarely at identifying risk and uncovering growth and churn-prevention opportunities — not just writing a nicer cold email.

Real needs, real use cases

Targeting

Segmenting accounts

Automatically classifying accounts as B2B or B2C, and surfacing the signals that matter for how a rep should approach each one.

Personalization

Emails grounded in real pain points

Crafting outreach by researching an account's actual challenges and aligning them with what the company offers — not a generic template with a name swapped in.

Account management

Plans that populate themselves

Auto-filling the account plan with the critical insights a rep would otherwise have to dig up and write manually.

Territory planning

Research at territory scale

Supporting territory planning and management by running research across many accounts at once, not one at a time.

Risk

Catching churn before it's obvious

Using first-party signals to detect stakeholder sentiment and churn indicators early — and just as importantly, what a rep should not spend time chasing.

The goal was never another dashboard. It was to make the account plan write itself — so a rep spends their time closing, not compiling.

What I'd tell another designer starting this today

  • An AI feature is sometimes a hedge against commoditization, not just a nice-to-have.
  • First-party data is the moat — anyone can bolt on web research alone.
  • More usage should make the product smarter, not just busier.
  • The best agent output still lets the human edit the last mile.
  • Sometimes the highest-value insight is what to ignore, not what to chase.
Outreach · Senior Product Designer

Smart Email Assist

Bringing generative AI into the sales workflow — six weeks, zero precedent, and a market that wouldn't wait.

Role
Design lead, end-to-end
Team
Product, Design, Eng, Data Science, Marketing
Timeline
Nov 2022 – Q1 2023
Surfaces
Web · Gmail · Outlook · Chrome

Salespeople spend roughly 28% of their time on non-selling work — chiefly reading and writing emails. In November 2022 I joined our product team shadowing Outreach sales reps in London, watching that pain up close. A month later, ChatGPT 3 shipped and turned a "three-to-four-years-out" concept into something we could build now.

Leadership wanted to unveil it at our sales conference. That gave us six weeks to go from idea to demo-ready prototype — so we scoped tightly to email replies, using the buyer's incoming message as grounding context for the AI draft.

Project highlights
Challenge

Bridging the gap

Reps needed AI help that sounded like their own voice and answered real prospect questions — not a generic chatbot reply.

Approach

Experience comes first

Scoped tightly, grounded generation in proprietary content, and shipped a working prototype in six weeks flat.

Outcome

Leading with differentiation

The first GenAI feature in Outreach's product — shipped on four surfaces, and the template for every AI feature since.

Designing under a deadline

My first instinct — a split button tucked in the corner of the compose window — matched patterns from Microsoft Copilot and GrammarlyGO. It didn't fit us. Users wanted to set tone, length, and prompt before generating, almost every time, and our pattern forced two levels of navigation to get there. Placement was inconsistent too: it didn't sit naturally alongside templates and snippets, and broke down across Gmail, Outlook, and our Chrome extension.

With the deadline closing in, we stepped back and wrote three principles instead: consistency (one toolbar, four surfaces), efficiency over distraction (faster than typing, or it's not worth shipping), and transparency & guidance (teach good prompting in the moment, and always ask users to review AI output before sending).

Five real challenges

Accuracy

One good draft wasn't realistic

Data Science told us a single accurate suggestion wasn't achievable yet. We shifted to three drafts — a "human in the loop" model I worried would slow people down. Research said the opposite: choosing between options felt like control, not friction.

Cost

Generation isn't free

Every input and output token has a real cost. We made generation opt-in per reply rather than automatic, so it triggered only when the AI actually earned its cost.

Competition

The floor moved overnight

Days after our conference debut, Microsoft announced Copilot and Google announced Bard. A first-mover moment suddenly had a lot of company.

Grounding

Public LLMs can't answer private questions

"Why is your product better than X?" isn't answered anywhere on the open internet. We built a content-recommendation layer that grounded drafts in each org's own templates and snippets — a moat competitors couldn't copy overnight.

Privacy

Trust had to be designed, not assumed

Legal required opt-in, not on-by-default. We built admin controls to toggle access per profile, plus clear in-product messaging that no personal or customer data is shared with ChatGPT.

"If you want to go fast, go alone. If you want to go far, go with your peers." That's exactly how this shipped — Product, Design, Engineering, Data Science, and Marketing, all in the same six weeks.

What I'd tell another designer starting this today

  • Shadow the real workflow before you design anything.
  • A tight deadline is a forcing function for principles, not just pixels.
  • "Human in the loop" is often a feature, not a compromise.
  • Your real moat is rarely the model — it's the proprietary context only you have.
  • Trust is a design problem. Opt-in doesn't have to mean low adoption.
Eurowag · Head of Design

Self-Service Credit, Built for a Public Company

Replacing a sales-led credit process with a self-service, AI-assisted application — while building the brand system Eurowag needed to go public on the LSE.

Role
Head of Design, hands-on + team leadership
Scope
Product strategy, AI application flow, design systems, brand identity
Surfaces
Credit application, brand system, playbook
Focus
Trust, escalation, scalability
<15 min
Time-to-decision, down from 3–4 business days
~65%
Applications resolved via self-service, no underwriter
3–4 teams
Adopted the self-service blueprint within 12 months
LSE
Brand consistency held through the public listing

The problem: growth was being sold to headcount

When I joined, the instinct for growing Eurowag's business credit line was the same one most B2B financial services default to: hire more sales reps, call more leads, close more deals by hand. It works, but it doesn't scale — every new market or product line meant another round of hiring, another ramp-up cycle, another ceiling.

I didn't think the constraint was sales capacity. I thought it was that we were asking a human to manually do something a well-designed flow could do faster and more consistently: qualify a business, walk it through a credit application, and get it a decision. This was before "AI agent" was a phrase anyone in the industry used seriously — I wasn't chasing a trend, I was trying to remove a bottleneck, and a self-service, AI-assisted application happened to be the right shape for the problem.

The bet: a self-service agent for something nobody self-serves

Business credit is not a low-stakes form. Getting a company comfortable applying for financing without a salesperson on the phone meant the flow had to do two things at once: feel fast enough that a business owner would actually finish it, and feel trustworthy enough that they'd hand over real financial information to a screen instead of a person. I worked closely with a product manager and engineering to keep scope tight rather than letting it sprawl into a full onboarding suite.

Scope

Collapsing to the minimum defensible set

Every additional field or screen is a place a business owner abandons the flow. Each step had to earn its place against what it actually changed about the credit decision — not what was convenient to ask for.

Transparency

Making the "why" of every ask visible

If we asked for a document or data point, the applicant could see why it mattered to their application. Opacity kills trust faster than friction does.

Escalation

A path to a human, not around one

Self-service didn't mean fully automated. Edge cases and declines routed to a real underwriter — the system's job was to handle the confidently-simple cases fast, not replace judgment on the ones that needed it.

It would have been simpler to either keep a human in every step, or automate the whole thing and accept the risk. I designed for the middle, because in lending, a system that's fast but wrong erodes trust faster than one that's occasionally slow.

The parallel track: designing a company that was about to go public

At the same time, Eurowag was moving from a founder- and private-equity-backed company into a business preparing to list on the London Stock Exchange — the shift from W.A.G Payment Solutions as a private operator to a publicly listed, FTSE-tracked company. That transition put design pressure on an entirely different surface: everything customer-, partner-, and investor-facing needed to read as one coherent, credible company, not a patchwork of product teams shipping independently.

I ran this in parallel with the credit product work rather than sequentially, because the business didn't have the luxury of doing one and then the other.

Product track

The self-service credit flow

A tight, trust-first application that turns a multi-day, sales-led process into a decision in minutes — with a clear escalation path built in from day one.

Brand & IPO track

A public company identity

A brand system flexible enough for product teams to apply consistently without a designer approving every instance — built to hold up under public-company scrutiny while still moving at startup speed internally.

The blueprint: making the switch repeatable, not a one-off

The credit application was one product. What the business actually needed was for every team to make this same switch — from manual, sales-assisted process to fast, self-service, AI-assisted product — without each team rediscovering the same lessons from scratch. So I turned what I'd learned into a repeatable playbook: how to decide what to automate versus escalate, how to design the "why" into an AI-assisted step, and how to build self-service that didn't just serve customers but served our own internal teams too — the people processing exceptions, handling support, and maintaining these flows day to day. Self-service that only helps the customer and leaves internal teams drowning in manual review isn't actually a solved problem; I wanted the blueprint to force both sides of that equation.

What I'd do differently

  • The blueprint should exist before the second team needs it, not get extracted after the first one ships.
  • Systems-thinking deserves its own explicit track from day one, not a trail behind the flagship product.
  • A team shouldn't learn a playbook at the same time you're still writing it down.
  • Self-service that helps customers but drowns internal teams in manual review isn't a solved problem.
